newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish arms company sees no need for new inquiry.
newsitem.headline: Swedish arms company sees no need for new inquiry.

text.p: Swedish arms maker Bofors said on Wednesday it saw no need to reopen an investigation into a 1986 artillery contract in India despite the naming of five people who received payments from the company.

After seven years of legal wrangling, Indian investigators last month received bank documents from Switzerland relating to the $1.3 billion artillery contract from which they released five names on Tuesday as recipients of money from Bofors.
Agneta Smed, a spokeswoman for Bofors, a unit of Swedish defence group Celsius, said the information was not new although Bofors has never released the names of its agents involved in the deal.
"We have always said we paid money to some people but this was not bribes," Smed told Reuters.
"It was final payments to some of our agents. The names of our agents remain classified."

A statement from India's Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) on Tuesday named Ottavio Quattrochi and his wife Maria, Win Chadha and his wife Kanta and son W.H. Chadha as recipients of payments from Bofors.
"The CBI is taking necessary steps to take action against the persons involved," the statement said, without elaborating.
Quattrocchi was the Indian representative of Italian engineering firm Snamprogetti SPA when the artillery contract between Bofors and the Indian government was signed in 1986.
Chadha was the Indian agent for Bofors.
Smed said Bofors was watching the Indian inquiry into the Swiss documents but saw no need to carry out its own investigations. It currently has no operations in India.
"We are not going to do any investigations ourselves for the time being but we will just wait and see," she said.
"We hope the investigation will lead to the embargo against Bofors operating in India being lifted."
Swiss police have said there was evidence Bofors paid about $40 million into various banks accounts in Switzerland during the time the contract with India was drawn up and settled.
The furore over the alleged payments contributed to the defeat in 1989 of the government led by late prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, who was accused of involvement in the affair.
India has been trying to discover whether leading Indian politicians took bribes in connection with the arms deal.
